hook.question: A set of Russian dolls is closed. You can only open one doll at a time, and you can't peek inside. How do you count how many dolls are in the set?
paragraphs: Open the big doll and you find a smaller doll that is a copy of the same puzzle: "how many dolls are inside this one?" So you ask that question again, on the smaller doll, and again, until you hold the tiniest doll, the one that doesn't open.
That tiniest doll is the only one that knows its answer without asking anybody. What does it say, and what does everyone above it do with that answer?
hook.aha: The tiniest doll says "just me, 1". Each doll above it says "1 plus whatever the doll inside me said" and passes the number back up. Nobody had to see the whole set: every doll solved one small step and trusted a smaller copy of itself for the rest. That is recursion.

metaphor: Picture a stack of sticky notes on your desk, one for every task you have started but not finished. When a task needs a smaller task done first, you stick a new note on top and work on that one. When the top note is finished, you tear it off and the note under it can carry on.
Backtracking is exploring a maze this way. At every fork you pick a corridor and walk in, and at a dead end you step back to the fork, undo that choice, and try the next corridor.
mentalModel.click: Don't follow every call in your head: solve one step, trust the smaller call to return the right answer, and make sure some call stops.

glossary.definition: The smallest version of the problem, answered directly with no further calls. Without it the calls never stop.
The step where the function calls itself on a smaller input and uses what comes back.
The pile of calls that have started but not finished. A new call goes on top, and returning removes it.
What happens when the stack gets too deep, usually from a missing base case or a huge input. The program crashes (Python stops at around a thousand calls by default).
Building an answer one choice at a time, and stepping back to undo a choice as soon as that branch is finished or cannot work.
The backtracking rhythm: add a choice to the path, recurse to see where it leads, then remove it so the next choice starts from a clean path.
Cutting off a branch as soon as you can tell it can't lead to a valid answer, so you never explore it.

mentalModel.definition: Recursion solves a problem by calling the same function on a smaller input until it reaches a base case that is answered directly, then combining the answers as the calls return. Backtracking is recursion over a tree of choices: each call chooses one option, explores everything that follows from it, and unchooses it before trying the next option. Pruning skips branches that can no longer succeed.

useWhen: The problem asks for all subsets, permutations, combinations or arrangements, so the answer is a list of lists of choices.
Every step has a few options, and you must be able to undo one to try the next.
The problem contains a smaller copy of itself: a tree, a nested structure, or "solve the left half and the right half".
The input is tiny (n of about 10 to 20), which says an exponential search is expected.
notWhen: You only need a count or a best value, and the same sub-problems keep coming back: dynamic programming remembers them instead of re-solving.
A simple rule is provably safe at each step, like always taking the meeting that ends first: greedy never needs to explore the other branches.
The depth could be 100,000 or more: plain recursion may overflow the stack, so loop or keep your own stack.

quiz.problem: Given an array of distinct integers, return all of its possible permutations.
quiz.explanation: You must list every arrangement, and each position is a choice you make and undo. That is backtracking.

quiz.problem: You climb stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Count the distinct ways to reach step 45, and return only the count.
quiz.explanation: Plain recursion would solve the same smaller staircases over and over. Remembering each answer once is dynamic programming.

quiz.problem: Given n pairs of parentheses, generate every well-formed combination of them.
quiz.explanation: Add ( or ) one at a time, undo it, and prune any branch that closes more than it opened. All combinations means backtracking.

quiz.problem: In a maze grid, find the fewest moves from the start to the exit.
quiz.explanation: Fewest moves on a grid means exploring level by level, which is a breadth-first search.

quiz.problem: Given meeting time intervals, find the most meetings one person can attend without overlap.
quiz.explanation: Taking the meeting that ends first is always safe, so there is no need to try every combination.

pseudocode.text: if i == n: save a copy of path, return (base case)
if path is shorter than the limit: (else prune)

notes: Every number is taken or skipped, so there are 2ⁿ leaves, and saving each subset copies up to n numbers: O(n · 2ⁿ) time.
Extra space is the call stack plus the path, both at most n deep: O(n). The list of answers is output, and it is not counted.
Save a copy of the path (path[:] in Python, new ArrayList<>(path) in Java). If you save the path itself, every saved answer is the same list, and unchoose empties it.
Unchoose must exactly undo choose. If it doesn't, the next branch starts from a dirty path and every answer after it is wrong.
Prune as early as you can: a branch cut near the root saves a whole subtree. With the limit, a full path never takes another number.

Plain recursion that re-solves the same sub-problem, like fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2), repeats work: fib(3) is computed twice inside fib(5). Remembering answers fixes it, and that is the dynamic-programming lesson.

examples.title: Fibonacci Number
examples.problem: The Fibonacci numbers start with F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1, and each next number is the sum of the two before it. Given n, return F(n).
approach: The base cases are n = 0 and n = 1: F(n) is n itself, no calls needed.
The recursive case is F(n) = F(n - 1) + F(n - 2), two calls on smaller inputs.
Written plainly, this solves the same F(k) again and again and takes exponential time.
Store each answer in a memo the first time you compute it, and the work drops to one call per k.

examples.title: Subsets
examples.problem: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The answer must not contain duplicate subsets, and may be in any order.
approach: Keep a path of the numbers chosen so far. Every path is a subset, so save a copy of it at the start of each call.
Loop over the numbers from start onwards: choose nums[i], recurse with i + 1 so you only go forward, then unchoose.
Going forward only means each subset is built in exactly one order, so there are no duplicates.
The stage replays the same tree as a take-or-skip choice per number: the answers are the same.

examples.title: Permutations
examples.problem: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all the possible permutations. You can return the answer in any order.
approach: A permutation uses every number once, so the path is complete when its length equals len(nums).
At each step try every number, but skip one that is already used. A used array remembers which.
Choose: mark it used and add it to the path. Explore: recurse. Unchoose: remove it and mark it unused.
There are n! answers and each copy costs up to n, so the time is O(n · n!).

conceptQuiz.question: What happens to a recursive function that has no base case?
options: It runs forever without using any extra memory.
Every call makes another call, the stack keeps growing, and the program crashes with a stack overflow.
The compiler adds a base case for you.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Each call goes on the stack and none ever returns. Memory for the stack runs out and the program stops.

conceptQuiz.question: In backtracking, what does the unchoose step do?
options: It undoes the last choice, so the path is back to what it was before and the next option starts clean.
It saves the current path into the answer.
It clears the whole path and starts again from the root.
It skips the rest of the loop.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Choose and unchoose are a matched pair. Because unchoose restores the path exactly, a branch can use the same path as its sibling.

conceptQuiz.question: Why do we save a copy of the path, like path[:], instead of the path itself?
options: Copies run faster than the original.
The path is one list that keeps changing. Saving it directly would store the same list many times, and unchoose would leave them all empty.
conceptQuiz.explanation: A saved reference would follow every later push and pop. A copy freezes the subset as it was at that moment.

conceptQuiz.question: What is the time of generating all subsets of n numbers, and why?
options: O(n), because each number is visited once.
O(n · 2ⁿ): there are 2ⁿ subsets and copying each one takes up to n steps.
O(2ⁿ), because copying a subset is free.
O(n²), because there are two nested choices.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Each number doubles the number of subsets, giving 2ⁿ of them. Writing each one into the answer costs up to n.

conceptQuiz.question: Why is fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) slow for a big n when written as plain recursion?
options: The base case is checked too often.
Each call makes two more calls, and the same smaller values are solved again and again.
conceptQuiz.explanation: fib(5) needs fib(3) twice, and the repeats multiply as n grows. Remembering the answers removes them, which is dynamic programming. Recursion itself is not always exponential: fact(n) makes n calls.

practice.title: Reverse Linked List
practice.insight: Trust that the call on head.next hands back a reversed rest of the list, then fix the one link between head and it.

practice.title: Pow(x, n)
practice.insight: A power is the square of a power half as big, so you can halve the problem instead of shrinking it by one. Watch negative n.

practice.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
practice.insight: The smaller head must come first. Its next is the merge of what remains: a smaller copy of the same problem.

practice.title: Combination Sum
practice.insight: A number may be reused, so recurse from the same index, and prune once the running sum passes the target.

practice.title: Combinations
practice.insight: Like subsets, but you stop when the path has k numbers. Think about when a branch can no longer reach k.

practice.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
practice.insight: Each digit is one level of the tree and its letters are the choices at that level.

practice.title: Generate Parentheses
practice.insight: Count how many ( and ) you have used. A ) is only allowed while there are more ( than ), and that rule is your pruning.

practice.title: N-Queens
practice.insight: Place one queen per row. Try each column, skip the ones that are attacked, and unchoose when a row has no safe spot.

overview: Explain how a base case stops a recursive call from running forever.
Trace the call stack for factorial as calls go down and return.
Implement a recursive function that solves a smaller copy of the problem.
Trace backtracking through subsets, choosing then unchoosing each element.
Prune a branch as soon as it cannot lead to a valid answer.
Spot why naive recursive Fibonacci repeats work and runs slowly.
